title: Talking to Claude
description: Write prompts that get great results on the first try.

lessons.title: Anatomy of a Great Prompt
lessons.description: Context, goal, constraints, definition of done.

theory.title: Four ingredients
theory.body:
Claude is smart, but it can't read your mind. A strong task prompt usually has:

**Context**: what's going on and where (`the checkout page in src/checkout/`).

**Goal**: the specific outcome you want.

**Constraints**: what to avoid or keep (`don't add dependencies`).

**Definition of done**: how you'll both know it worked (`all tests in cart.test.ts pass`).
theory.code:
Users report the cart total is wrong when a coupon is applied.
Fix the calculation in src/cart/total.ts.
Don't change the public function signatures.
Done = existing tests pass and you add a test for the coupon case.

theory.title: Specific beats short
theory.body: "fix the bug" forces Claude to guess which bug. Every guess burns time and tokens. A couple of extra sentences up front saves several rounds of back-and-forth. Kip calls this "measure twice, prompt once".

exercises.prompt: You want Claude to fix a failing test.
options: The test 'applies coupon' in src/cart/total.test.ts fails since yesterday's refactor. Find the cause and fix the code, not the test. Done when npm test passes.
exercises.explanation: The better prompt names the test, the likely cause, a constraint, and a clear finish line.

exercises.prompt: Match each prompt fragment to the ingredient it provides.

pairs.left: "in the settings page of our React app"
"done when the toggle persists on reload"

exercises.explanation: Context, goal, constraints and a definition of done together remove guesswork.

exercises.prompt: Which addition most improves the prompt "make the API faster"?
options: Naming the slow endpoint and a target, e.g. GET /users under 200ms
exercises.explanation: A concrete target and location turns a vague wish into a measurable task.

exercises.scenario: Your Express API's GET /users endpoint returns every user at once and is getting slow. You want page-based pagination added without breaking the existing mobile client.
exercises.sample: Add pagination to GET /users in @src/api/users.ts. Accept ?page and ?limit query params (default limit 20, max 100) and return { data, page, total }. Keep the default response compatible for the mobile client when no params are sent. Add tests in @src/api/users.test.ts; done when npm test passes.
exercises.explanation: A great prompt names the file, the exact behavior, the compatibility constraint, and how success is checked.

exercises.prompt: Fill in the missing ingredients of this prompt template.
exercises.code:
Context: the login form in src/auth/
___: show an error when the password is wrong
___: don't change the API client
Done ___: the error renders and tests pass
exercises.explanation: Goal, constraint, and a 'done when' line complete the four-part prompt.

exercises.prompt: Why include a definition of done?
options: It tells Claude how to verify its work and when to stop
exercises.explanation: A clear finish line, like passing tests, lets Claude check its own work.

exercises.prompt: You want a new feature added to a component.
options: Add a 'copy link' button to the ShareMenu component in src/components/ShareMenu.tsx. Use the existing Button component and show a 'Copied!' toast for 2 seconds.
can you add some sharing stuff
exercises.explanation: Naming the component, the reusable pieces, and the exact behavior gets it right in one pass.

theory.title: @ means "look here"
theory.body:
Type `@` followed by a path to pull a file into the conversation: `@src/utils/date.ts`. Press `Tab` to autocomplete paths, so you don't have to remember them.

Reference a whole directory with a trailing slash: `@src/components/`.

Referencing files saves Claude from searching and makes your intent unambiguous.
theory.code:
> Explain how @src/auth/session.ts refreshes tokens
> What does each file in @src/hooks/ do?

exercises.prompt: Ask Claude to explain the file src/utils/date.ts by referencing it directly. Type: explain @ followed by the path.
exercises.hint: No space between @ and the path.
exercises.explanation: @path/to/file pulls that file into the conversation so Claude doesn't have to hunt for it.

exercises.prompt: How do you reference an entire directory?
exercises.explanation: The @ prefix with a directory path references the folder and its structure.

exercises.prompt: You can't remember the exact path after typing @src/au. What helps?
exercises.explanation: Tab completion works on @ file paths.

exercises.prompt: Reference a file and a folder in one prompt.
exercises.code: Refactor ___src/api/client.ts to use the helpers in ___src/lib/
exercises.explanation: The @ prefix works for both files and directories.

exercises.prompt: You want Claude to update the date formatting helper.
options: Update the date thing somewhere in utils so it shows the weekday
Update formatDate in @src/utils/date.ts so it includes the short weekday, e.g. 'Mon, 3 Mar'
exercises.explanation: An @ reference plus an example output leaves nothing to guess.

exercises.scenario: The signup form accepts invalid emails. Validation lives in a shared validators file, and the form component uses it. Ask Claude to fix it.
exercises.sample: In @src/lib/validators.ts, isValidEmail accepts strings like 'a@b' with no TLD. Tighten it to require a domain with a dot, update @src/components/SignupForm.tsx to show the error under the field, and add unit tests for valid and invalid cases. Don't change the function's signature.
exercises.explanation: Referencing both files with @ and describing the bad input makes the fix precise.

exercises.prompt: Match each reference to what Claude receives.
exercises.explanation: File paths pull in a file, while a trailing slash points at a folder.

lessons.title: Show, Don't Describe
lessons.description: Paste errors, screenshots, and command output.

theory.title: Paste the real thing
theory.body:
Don't paraphrase an error. **Paste the full error text or stack trace** straight into the prompt. Exact messages and line numbers are gold.

For UI bugs or mockups, **paste an image** with `Ctrl+V` or drag and drop a screenshot into the terminal.

Need command output in the chat? Start a line with `!` to run a shell command directly (bash mode), and its output lands in the conversation.
theory.code:
> ! npm test
> The test above fails, fix the cause, not the test

exercises.prompt: Your build crashes. What do you send?
options: The build has some type error about undefined, can you look?

Build fails with:
TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'map')
    at ProductList (src/components/ProductList.tsx:42:18)
Fix the root cause.
exercises.explanation: The exact error and stack trace point Claude to the file and line immediately.

exercises.prompt: How do you paste a screenshot into Claude Code?
options: Ctrl+V (or drag and drop the image)
exercises.explanation: Claude Code accepts pasted or dragged-in images, which is great for UI bugs and mockups.

exercises.prompt: Run git status directly from the Claude prompt using bash mode.
exercises.hint: Start the line with an exclamation mark.
exercises.explanation: The ! prefix runs a shell command directly and adds its output to the conversation.

exercises.prompt: Order an efficient bug report to Claude.
steps: Copy the full error or stack trace
Add what you expected to happen
Ask Claude to find and fix the root cause
exercises.explanation: Real evidence plus expected behavior gives Claude everything to diagnose the issue.

exercises.prompt: Match the input to the best way to share it.
exercises.explanation: Each kind of evidence has a fast, lossless way into the conversation.

exercises.scenario: Your header navigation overlaps the logo on mobile widths. You have a screenshot of the bug and know the header lives in one component file.
exercises.sample: [screenshot pasted] On screens under 400px the nav links in @src/components/Header.tsx overlap the logo, as shown. Fix the layout in @src/styles/header.css so links collapse into the existing hamburger menu below 640px. Don't change the desktop layout.
exercises.explanation: A screenshot plus a file reference and a constraint makes a visual bug easy to fix.

exercises.prompt: Why paste the exact error instead of summarizing it?
options: Exact messages include file paths, line numbers and details a summary loses
exercises.explanation: The precise text carries the clues Claude needs to locate the problem.

lessons.title: Plan Before Code
lessons.description: Ask for a plan, review it, then build.

theory.title: Think first, type later
theory.body:
For anything bigger than a one-liner, ask Claude to **explore and plan before writing code**. Say it outright: `don't write any code yet`.

You review the plan, poke holes in it, and only then say go. Fixing a plan costs one message, while fixing a wrong implementation costs many.

You can also nudge Claude to reason harder by asking it to **think** through tricky problems.
theory.code:
> Read @src/billing/ and propose a plan to add yearly plans.
> Don't write any code yet. List the files you'd change and why.

exercises.prompt: You need to migrate the app from REST calls to a GraphQL client.
options: Look through @src/api/ and propose a step-by-step plan to migrate to our GraphQL client. Don't write code yet; list files, risks, and the order of changes.
exercises.explanation: For a big change, a reviewed plan prevents expensive wrong turns.

exercises.prompt: Order the plan-first workflow.
steps: Ask Claude to read the relevant code
Ask for a plan and say don't write code yet
Tell Claude to implement the plan
exercises.explanation: Explore, plan, review, implement, verify: the order matters.

exercises.prompt: When is asking for a plan LEAST necessary?
options: Fixing a typo in a README
exercises.explanation: Trivial, well-scoped changes don't need a planning round.

exercises.prompt: Complete the plan-first prompt.
exercises.code:
Read @src/billing/ and propose a ___ for yearly plans.
Don't write any ___ yet.
exercises.explanation: Asking for a plan and explicitly holding off on code keeps Claude in exploration mode.

exercises.scenario: You want to add role-based access control (admin, editor, viewer) to an existing Next.js app. You don't want any code written until you've approved an approach.
exercises.sample: Read @src/lib/auth.ts and @src/middleware.ts and propose a plan to add role-based access control with admin, editor and viewer roles. Don't write code yet. Cover where roles are stored, how middleware checks them, which routes need protection (e.g. @src/app/admin/page.tsx), and how we'll test it.
exercises.explanation: Pointing Claude at the key files and asking for a reviewed plan sets up a safe, large change.

exercises.prompt: Claude's plan touches a file you want left alone. What now?
options: Tell Claude to revise the plan without touching that file
exercises.explanation: Correcting the plan is cheap, so fix it before any code exists.

exercises.prompt: Match the phrase to its purpose.
exercises.explanation: These phrases move Claude from exploration to execution on your terms.

mission.title: Prompt Smith
mission.intro: Forge a real prompt on a real codebase and see the difference specificity makes.
checklist: Pick a small real task and write a prompt with context, goal, constraints and a definition of done
Reference at least one file with @ (use Tab to autocomplete the path)
Paste a real error message or screenshot into the prompt
Ask Claude for a plan with "don't write code yet", correct it once, then let it implement
mission.explanation: Clear, grounded prompts plus a reviewed plan are the fastest path to correct code.

cheatsheet.description: The four ingredients of a strong task prompt.
Pull a file into the conversation; Tab autocompletes.
Paste an image; drag and drop also works.
Bash mode: run a shell command and add its output.
Exact stack traces beat paraphrased descriptions.
Ask for a plan first and review it before building.
Nudge Claude to reason more carefully on hard problems.
